newsitem.title: USA: CME board Feb 5 to mull cutting Eurodlr tick size.
newsitem.headline: CME board Feb 5 to mull cutting Eurodlr tick size.

text.p: The Chicago Mercantile Exchange board of directors will discuss whether to halve the minimum tick size in some Eurodollar futures when it meets Wednesday, CME president-designate Rick Kilcollin said.
"The proposal will go to the board next week, so we'll see," Kilcollin said in an interview.

Until recently, all Eurodollar futures were quoted in full basis points, or increments of 0.01 each worth $25.00. The CME already has tested half-ticks, or 0.005 basis points each worth $12.50, with the January 1997 Eurodollar contract that expired last week.
CME will implement half-ticks for the February contract Monday when it goes into delivery month, with the aim of increasing volume and tightening the bid-ask spread, he said.

"What tends to happen is, maybe the market is bid at three and offered at four and there are 3,000, 4,000 or 5,000 contracts on both sides but not much trading going on," Kilcollin explained. "We would bring more buyers and sellers together (by narrowing the spread)."
He said there was no decision yet on which contracts would be affected by the possible change but that he doubted if all expiration months would be quoted in half-ticks.
Floor brokers have said the CME is also considering quoting serial-month and some quarterly expirations in quarter-ticks, or increments of $0.0025 each worth $6.25.

Kilcollin, due to take office next week, noted that the measure was part of a drive to improve the Eurodollar contract. Other steps being considered included modifying the configuration and size of the trading pit and reducing exchange-charged fees.
"Markets are always evolving rapidly and I think we have to evolve ourselves to be competitive," he said.
Kilcollin said one basis point was the smallest minimum tick size among U.S. short-term interest contracts when the Eurodollar contract was originally created.

"Spreads everywhere have come in," he said. "So we're finding that in order to remain competitive in the marketplace, we need to lower the spreads as other spreads in the market are coming down," he said.
